# Decoding the 7.6V Mystery on a 2010 Chevy Malibu PCM

Encountering a "no crank/no start" condition where the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) is only receiving 7.6 volts immediately points to a specific failure mode in the ignition power distribution network. On the 2010 Chevy Malibu with the 2.4L engine, this voltage sag at pin D12 (pink and black wire) on connector X2 of the fuse box is not merely a low-voltage event; it indicates an open circuit or a high-resistance path where a stable battery voltage should exist.

The symptom you describedâmeasuring 7.6V at the PCM input and subsequently finding 4.7kÎ© resistance between pin D12 and terminal 30 of relay 33âis the smoking gun. In a healthy automotive electrical system, we expect near-zero resistance for power feed circuits. A reading of 4.7kÎ© confirms that the path is open or severely compromised. This high impedance prevents the PCM from pulling enough current to initialize its internal logic and fire the fuel injectors. Consequently, the engine will not crank because the starter solenoid often shares this power rail (POW/TRN circuit), or the PCM lacks the necessary voltage to energize the ignition coil drivers.

The diagnostic journey here involves tracing the power supply chain upstream from the PCM. Relay 33 is responsible for switching the main battery voltage to these sensitive components. When you measured 7.6V at the relay itself, it suggests the issue might be downstream of the relay contacts or within the relay's internal coil mechanism if it were a control issue, but your resistance check clarifies the topology. The 4.7kÎ© reading between the input side (D12) and the output terminal implies the continuity path is broken before it reaches the PCM.

Tracing this wire backward reveals the architecture of the vehicle's primary power distribution. The feed for relay 33 typically originates from a dedicated fuse in the main under-hood fuse block, often protected by a high-amperage blade or fusible link. If you cannot locate the upstream source in your wiring diagrams, it is common to find that the "feed" enters the relay box via a specific input terminal on the back of the relay socket.

Once the ground strap connecting the engine block near the starter was identified and restored, the vehicle began cranking, validating that the chassis ground path was indeed critical to the PCM's operation. However, the persistence of code P1682 (PCM Power Relay Control Circuit Malfunction) and the lack of injector pulse indicate a secondary failure or an incomplete repair. The fact that you replaced the PCM initially suggests that the high-resistance connection mimicked a dead module. Even with a fresh PCM, if the voltage rail is unstable due to corrosion, loose terminals, or a failing main fuse, the new unit will immediately fault out again.

When addressing P1682 and injector pulse loss after restoring ground, consider checking the resistance of the fuel pump relay and ensuring the main battery cable connections at the starter motor are clean and tight. A weak connection at the battery can cause voltage sag under load that mimics a PCM failure. Additionally, verify that the fuel pump relay is receiving its control signal; if the PCM cannot communicate with the fuel pump relay due to the ground issue it just resolved, the P1682 code will remain active until the communication loop is fully verified.
